attacks_proposed.argument: The no-causation theory assumes the very proposition in dispute: that Lundberg would legally have become unsecured even if the release was invalid. An expectation that a document would be filed does not itself extinguish a lien. Ohio proximate cause requires a reasonable connection between the defendant’s act and the plaintiff’s damage. If the release was ineffective, Land Title cannot eliminate that connection merely by invoking Lundberg’s supposed expectation; it must establish what legally caused the loss of the security interest. The brief instead declares the release’s validity immaterial while making the entire causation analysis depend on the release having the same practical effect as a valid discharge.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If an invalid release did not alter the lien, the premise that Lundberg was already destined to be unsecured fails, leaving a genuine causation issue that defeats summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief supplies no authority establishing that this unrecorded release extinguished the mortgage upon signing or delivery. Its own formulation repeatedly says the release could have been filed and that, had it been filed, it would have extinguished the lien. That hypothetical does not prove that the unfiled instrument already produced the same legal result. Ohio authority treating an unrecorded deed as capable of passing title is expressly deed-specific and does not establish the legal effect of an unrecorded mortgage release. On summary judgment, Land Title had to establish its entitlement as a matter of law rather than leave the dispositive legal premise unsupported.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without a demonstrated rule making the unrecorded release operative, the trial court could not treat the lien as extinguished or use that conclusion to eliminate causation.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief overstates the release’s text by asserting that it releases Kevin and Christine Sheridan from all liability relating to the mortgage. The language actually quoted says only that the described property is released and discharged from the liens. That is not a release of the borrowers’ personal liability on the note. Because proximate causation concerns the reasonable connection between the challenged act and the particular damage claimed, the court cannot broaden a property-lien release into a complete discharge of all mortgage-related liability.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The overreading obscures the distinction between loss of collateral and continued liability on the debt, undermining the assertion that the release necessarily placed Lundberg in precisely the same position later produced by Land Title’s conduct.

attacks_proposed.argument: The claim that the parties did not dispute an intent to make Lundberg unsecured is not established by the cited testimony. The quoted evidence states Kevin Sheridan’s understanding that the purpose was to remove the mortgage and that other repayment arrangements existed. It does not quote Lundberg agreeing that the release was presently effective, that he intended to surrender the security interest regardless of filing, or that he possessed authority to bind Equity Trust. At summary judgment, evidence and reasonable inferences must be construed for the nonmovant, and the movant must affirmatively demonstrate the absence of supporting evidence rather than convert one participant’s understanding into an undisputed bilateral intent.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If Lundberg’s intent, the conditions attached to the release, or the contemplated legal effect remained disputed, Land Title could not use Kevin Sheridan’s testimony to establish no injury as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: The categorical assertion that only Equity Trust may recover damages does not follow merely from its designation as mortgagee. The amended complaint, as quoted by the brief, identifies Lundberg as the IRA’s beneficial owner. Ohio authority recognizes that a person with a beneficial interest may in appropriate circumstances enforce rights even though another person is the named contracting party. Conversely, authority requiring an ownership interest does not establish that record title is the only cognizable interest. Land Title therefore had to address whether Lundberg’s alleged beneficial ownership gave him a personal injury or enforceable interest; the absence of a written assignment alone does not resolve that question.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If beneficial ownership can support Lundberg’s claimed injury, the named-mortgagee premise does not establish lack of standing, and Land Title’s alternative ground fails.

attacks_proposed.argument: The apparent-authority theory lacks evidence of the required manifestation by the asserted principal, Equity Trust. The authority quoted in the brief itself asks whether the party to be bound caused the third party reasonably to believe that the purported agent possessed authority. But the evidence identified here consists of Lundberg’s signature, Lundberg’s delivery of the release, and Kevin Sheridan’s resulting belief. The brief identifies no words or conduct by Equity Trust that created or ratified that belief. A purported agent’s own representations cannot, without more, satisfy a requirement directed to the principal’s manifestations.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without evidence attributable to Equity Trust, apparent authority cannot validate the release as a matter of law, so it cannot supply the foundation for summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The cited testimony does not establish reasonable, detrimental reliance as a matter of law. Kevin Sheridan said only that the parties made other arrangements, continued trying to do business, and contemplated rehabilitation work. The brief does not identify undisputed evidence that he actually performed uncompensated work, surrendered another right, made a payment because of the release, or otherwise materially changed position in reliance on Lundberg’s supposed authority. His subjective belief that the document could be recorded is not itself proof of detrimental reliance.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Absent an established change of position, estoppel cannot independently bind Lundberg or cure the missing evidence of actual or apparent authority.

attacks_proposed.argument: Authority to enforce an interest and authority to relinquish it are not logically identical. A beneficial owner may possess standing based on injury to his beneficial interest while a separate custodian retains formal authority to execute a release. The brief’s own description distinguishes Lundberg as beneficial owner from Equity Trust as named mortgagee, yet its alternative argument collapses those distinct roles without authority showing that one power necessarily includes the other.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Rejecting that equivalence defeats the claim that a finding of standing automatically validates Lundberg’s attempted release.

attacks_proposed.argument: The proposed two-option framework is not exhaustive. A third legally coherent possibility is that Lundberg had a sufficient beneficial interest to suffer and sue for his own injury, while Equity Trust retained exclusive formal authority to discharge the mortgage. The brief’s own allegations identify Lundberg as beneficial owner and Equity Trust as custodian and mortgagee. Summary judgment cannot rest on declaring that these distinct interests must belong entirely to one or the other party.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Once the false dichotomy is removed, neither lack of standing nor validity of the release necessarily follows, and the admitted factual disputes become material.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief concedes factual disputes concerning who signed the mortgage and with what authority, yet declares them immaterial solely because of its release theory. That conclusion holds only if Land Title first establishes that the release was legally effective or that Lundberg indisputably would have lost the lien independently of Land Title’s acts. Because those predicates remain unsupported or disputed, the circumstances surrounding the filing may bear directly on whether there is a reasonable causal connection between Land Title’s conduct and the claimed loss. Ohio’s summary-judgment standard requires doubts and competing inferences to be resolved for the nonmovant.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the release issue is unresolved, the conceded disputes concerning the mortgage’s execution and filing cannot be dismissed as immaterial, and summary judgment must be reversed.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes the central circularity in Land Title's causation theory. The general Ohio causation proposition is supported: there must be a reasonable connection between the challenged conduct and the claimed loss. But neither that principle nor the cited summary-judgment standard establishes that Lundberg's subjective expectation has the legal effect of extinguishing security. If the release was unauthorized or otherwise ineffective, the fact that Lundberg expected it to be filed does not by itself place him in the same legal position as an unsecured creditor. Because the brief expressly says release validity is immaterial while deriving no injury from the release's intended effect, this attack directly threatens the principal ground for affirmance.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Lundberg knowingly signed and delivered the release, expected it to be filed, agreed to alternative repayment arrangements, and therefore is no worse off even if the release was invalid.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The decisive research is Ohio law on whether an unauthorized or ineffective mortgage release, coupled with delivery and intent that it be recorded, can itself eliminate damages or break causation.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands forcefully because the brief offers no authority on the dispositive legal effect of an unrecorded mortgage release. Its language is internally revealing: it repeatedly says the release could have been recorded and that, had it been recorded, the lien would have been extinguished. The retrieved deed authority does not answer the mortgage-release question, and the summary-judgment authority only states the burden. A court could supply the governing law independently, so the omission is not automatically fatal, but Land Title has not demonstrated from its cited authorities that signing or delivery alone discharged the lien. If Ohio law requires recording or some additional act, the trial court's valid-release premise cannot stand on this briefing.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief calls the release valid on its face, says Kevin received the original and could have recorded it at any time, and says filing would have immediately extinguished the lien. It cites no release or recording law.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research the version of R.C. 5301.28 and related Ohio mortgage-satisfaction law applicable in 2007, including whether an executed and delivered but unrecorded release is effective between the parties and against later interests.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's own cited apparent-authority cases support this attack more than Land Title's application. Master Consolidated and Miller frame apparent authority in terms of manifestations by the party to be bound—the principal. Here that principal would be Equity Trust, but the identified proof consists of Lundberg's execution and delivery of the document and Sheridan's belief. Those are manifestations by the purported agent, not Equity Trust. Unless the governing custodial documents, prior dealings, ratification, or some other conduct attributable to Equity Trust supplied the appearance of authority, apparent authority was not established as a matter of law. The generic summary-judgment source attached to the attack adds little, but the defect is apparent from Land Title's own authorities and record description.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that Lundberg's signed, witnessed, notarized release and his delivery of the original caused Sheridan reasonably to believe Lundberg had authority. It also says Equity Trust never appeared or denied Lundberg's authority.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Examine the IRA custodial agreement, account authorization documents, Equity Trust communications, and Ohio decisions addressing whether a principal's silence or placement of an agent in a particular position supplied apparent authority to release a mortgage.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief does overstate the record by calling bilateral intent undisputed when the quoted testimony chiefly establishes Kevin Sheridan's understanding. At summary judgment, Sheridan's understanding cannot simply be attributed to Lundberg. Still, Land Title has a substantial answer: Lundberg admitted knowingly signing a document expressly releasing the property, had it witnessed and notarized, and the record attributes delivery of the original to him. That conduct is strong objective evidence of an intent to release, even without a quoted admission about every legal consequence. The attack becomes serious only if there is admissible evidence of a condition on delivery, a different intended use, or lack of authority that prevents Lundberg's conduct from carrying its ordinary meaning.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on the release's text, Lundberg's admitted signature, Kevin Sheridan's testimony that Lundberg delivered the original, and testimony about alternative repayment arrangements. It does not quote Lundberg expressly agreeing that he would be unsecured regardless of recording or authority.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review Lundberg's complete deposition and any communications surrounding execution and delivery for evidence of conditions, limited purpose, mistake, or a contrary understanding.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's binary formulation is not logically compelled by its cited standing and agency cases. Standing to seek redress for injury to a beneficial interest and formal authority to execute a release on behalf of the record mortgagee are analytically different questions. Thus, the pleaded distinction between Lundberg as beneficial owner and Equity Trust as custodian leaves a possible middle position. But the attack does not establish that Ohio law actually gives an IRA beneficiary an individual cause of action concerning an asset legally held by the custodian. The sources cited for the attack are not specific to custodial IRAs or mortgage rights. The court would treat this as a real gap in Land Title's dichotomy, not as proof that Lundberg has standing.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Lundberg cannot have it both ways: if Equity Trust alone held the mortgage and alone could release it, Lundberg cannot enforce it; if Lundberg can enforce it, he must also have actual or apparent authority to release it.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research Ohio and federal authority defining ownership, litigation rights, and transactional authority for self-directed IRA assets held by a custodian, as well as Civ.R. 17(A)'s application to beneficial owners.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a valid limitation on the brief's estoppel theory. The cited testimony shows an asserted agreement for alternative repayment and continued business dealings, but the excerpts do not establish that Sheridan actually performed rehabilitation work, surrendered a claim, paid consideration, or otherwise changed position detrimentally because he believed Lundberg had authority. That prevents equitable estoppel from being established conclusively on the excerpts provided. The point does not independently defeat the judgment, however, because Land Title separately invokes actual authority, apparent authority, and causation; apparent authority also may involve reliance through entering the transaction even if the separate requirements of equitable estoppel are not met.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Sheridan accepted the release, agreed to alternative repayment through rehabilitation work, and continued the business relationship. It does not identify completed performance or another concrete detrimental change of position.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the full record for proof that Sheridan performed services, incurred obligations, relinquished remedies, or otherwise materially changed position after receiving the release.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief does not fully analyze Lundberg's pleaded status as beneficial owner, so there is a genuine unanswered question. But this proposed attack goes too far in suggesting that the retrieved authorities recognize a beneficial owner's right to recover on these facts. The cited eviction and third-party-beneficiary materials do not address self-directed IRA assets, custodial ownership, mortgage enforcement, or claims for impairment of a lien. On the present sources, beneficial ownership is an allegation requiring legal analysis, not an established basis for standing. The court would not reject Land Title's standing argument merely because the complaint used that label.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes the complaint's allegation that Lundberg sued individually and as beneficial owner, but emphasizes that Equity Trust is the named mortgagee, made no assignment, granted no documented power of attorney, and is not a party.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Specific authority on self-directed IRA custodians and Civ.R. 17(A) could materially change this assessment.

judge_assessments.assessment: The abstract proposition is correct: authority to enforce and authority to release are not necessarily identical. But this attack substantially duplicates the more complete false-dichotomy challenge in a9 and relies on sources that do not establish the allocation of powers between this IRA beneficiary and custodian. Standing alone, it identifies a logical gap without supplying the governing rule needed to decide the case.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief treats enforcement authority and release authority as coextensive and argues that Lundberg cannot claim one without the other.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The same IRA-ownership and agency research identified for a9 would settle the point.

judge_assessments.assessment: The quoted release does discharge the property from the lien, not the Sheridans' personal liability on the note, so u43's statement about release from all liability is textually overbroad. But the brief repeatedly recognizes that the debt survived and describes Lundberg as an unsecured creditor entitled to repayment through other arrangements. The brief's actual causation theory concerns loss of collateral, not elimination of the debt. The court would likely treat the sentence as imprecise drafting rather than a material distortion affecting the outcome.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Although u43 says the release discharged all liability relative to the mortgage, the brief elsewhere repeatedly states that Sheridan still owed the loan and that Lundberg merely became unsecured.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is derivative of the stronger attacks on the release's legal effect and causation. The disputes over who signed Christine Sheridan's name and with what authority may affect the mortgage's validity and Land Title's alleged breach, but they do not automatically establish that Land Title caused Lundberg's claimed loss. Even if the release theory fails, Lundberg still must connect the challenged filing conduct to a compensable impairment of an interest he owned. The court would first resolve the release, ownership, and causation questions rather than deem every conceded execution dispute material.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief concedes disputes concerning Christine's signature and Kevin's authority but argues they are immaterial because Lundberg signed and delivered a release intended to eliminate the lien and therefore suffered no loss attributable to Land Title.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The claims and damages allegations in Lundberg's amended complaint, together with the mortgage's treatment after filing, would show whether any particular execution dispute could affect his injury.

results.verdict: partly persuasive but vulnerable on the central legal and ca
results.assessment: The brief has a usable factual core: it shows Lundberg signed, notarized, and delivered a Release of Lien, which supports the narrative that the transaction was meant to release the lien. But it is exposed where it matters most. First, the causation theory is circular because it treats the release as legally effective while saying its validity is immaterial. Second, the briefing does not supply authority showing that an unrecorded mortgage release was already effective on signing or delivery. Third, the apparent-authority and intent arguments lean on Lundberg’s own conduct and Sheridan’s understanding, not a principal-side manifestation by Equity Trust, and the record is overstated as undisputed on bilateral intent. The research did not settle whether Ohio law requires recording for this release to be effective.

challenges.judge_assessment: The logic of this attack is sound. Land Title repeatedly says that filing the release would have extinguished the lien and thereby supplies the counterfactual for its no-injury theory. If Lundberg lacked authority and the release was ineffective, filing it would not necessarily have extinguished Equity Trust's interest. The brief tries to avoid that problem by shifting from legal effectiveness to Lundberg's supposed expectation that the release would be filed, but that expectation is itself a disputed inference and does not automatically establish the legal or damages baseline. The advocate risks losing summary judgment on proximate cause if release validity or Lundberg's informed intent remains genuinely disputed.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if the parties dispute the legal effect of the Release of Lien, that dispute does not establish damages from Land Title. The record shows that Lundberg voluntarily signed and delivered a release identifying the very mortgage at issue, and Kevin Sheridan testified that the parties had made other arrangements to pay back the loan. The alleged injury therefore cannot be traced to Land Title's accommodation filing, because Lundberg has not shown a cognizable loss caused by that filing rather than by the arrangement reflected in his own release.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that release validity is immaterial. Instead, say that even if the legal effect of the release is disputed, Land Title still prevails because the record shows Lundberg signed and delivered a release and the parties had already arranged an alternate repayment path; there is no record-supported injury from the filing itself.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief conflates authority to release Equity Trust's mortgage with standing to assert Lundberg's own tort claims against Land Title. The claims identified by the brief include fraud, negligent misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty, and breach of notarial duty, not merely an action to foreclose or enforce the mortgage. The standing authorities recited in the brief establish only the general requirement of standing and the purpose of the real-party-in-interest rule; they do not establish the asserted proposition that inability personally to execute a release necessarily eliminates any personal claim for injury caused by Land Title. Ohio law also recognizes that formal ownership is not invariably the sole test of real-party-in-interest status, as an authorized managing agent may qualify in the relevant statutory context.
challenges.why_it_matters: Land Title's alternative ground fails unless it separately analyzes Lundberg's interest and alleged injury under each asserted claim rather than assuming that mortgage-release authority and tort standing are identical.

target.excerpt: If Appellant Lundberg does not have the authority to release the lien at issue, then he also does not have the authority (necessary standing) to enforce it, entitling Land Title to summary judgment on this alternative basis.

challenges.judge_assessment: Land Title's categorical preservation position is inadequately supported. The assignments expressly challenge summary judgment, the finding of a valid release, and cancellation of the mortgage. An appellant ordinarily may argue why an appellee's alternative apparent-authority theory does not sustain those rulings without separately seeking reversal of the order striking a sur-reply. Moreover, Land Title affirmatively asks the appellate court to affirm on apparent authority, making it difficult to exclude all responsive legal argument. Still, the court may decline a distinct factual or legal theory not fairly presented below, and the record supplied does not conclusively show what authority arguments preceded the sur-replies. challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rely on a categorical waiver bar. Reframe the point as one of scope: the strike orders are not themselves assigned as error, but the Court can still affirm on the properly preserved summary-judgment record, and the apparent-authority discussion does not change the proximate-cause analysis.

challenges.opponent_argument: Land Title does not establish the essential causal premise of its motion. Its accommodation filing occurred on February 20, 2007, while the asserted release was not signed until March 1, 2007. A later document does not, by itself, negate a reasonable causal connection between the earlier filing and any injury already produced by that filing. Ohio proximate causation requires a reasonable connection between the defendant's act or omission and the damage; the challenged act need not be the initial or sole cause. Land Title instead treats the later release as automatically eliminating causation without identifying the alleged injuries, when they arose, or whether they would have occurred absent the filing.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without an injury-specific causal analysis, Land Title did not carry its summary-judgment burden on proximate cause merely by producing a later release.

judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief argues that only Equity Trust, as holder, can enforce the lien or recover damages flowing from it; that Equity Trust is absent; and that no assignment or power of attorney was produced. It relies on general standing cases and Triplett's explanation of the real-party-in-interest rule.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The amended third-party complaint, the alleged damages for each count, Civ.R. 17(A), and authority addressing beneficial owners of custodial IRAs would determine whether Lundberg has any personal cause of action.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes a genuine summary-judgment vulnerability, but the brief has substantial contrary evidence. Kevin Sheridan's quoted response does not expressly adopt counsel's proposition that Lundberg knowingly became unsecured; it confirms only that other repayment arrangements existed. Sheridan's understanding alone cannot conclusively establish Lundberg's state of mind. Still, Lundberg's acknowledged execution, notarization, and delivery of a document expressly releasing the identified lien provide strong objective evidence of intent. The attack becomes serious only if the record contains contrary testimony or evidence from Lundberg. Otherwise, a court could find the document and delivery sufficient despite Sheridan's equivocal answer. The advocate risks losing the undisputed no-injury baseline, not necessarily the entire case.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on the release's text, Lundberg's admitted signature, witnessing and notarization, delivery of the original to Sheridan, Sheridan's testimony about alternative repayment arrangements, and testimony that the release could have been recorded at any time.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Lundberg's complete deposition testimony about why he signed and delivered the release, and any evidence concerning conditions on its use, would likely control.

judge_assessments.assessment: Land Title's categorical preservation position is inadequately supported. The assignments expressly challenge summary judgment, the finding of a valid release, and cancellation of the mortgage. An appellant ordinarily may argue why an appellee's alternative apparent-authority theory does not sustain those rulings without separately seeking reversal of the order striking a sur-reply. Moreover, Land Title affirmatively asks the appellate court to affirm on apparent authority, making it difficult to exclude all responsive legal argument. Still, the court may decline a distinct factual or legal theory not fairly presented below, and the record supplied does not conclusively show what authority arguments preceded the sur-replies. The advocate risks losing a waiver shortcut and having apparent authority reviewed on the merits.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the no-apparent-authority argument first appeared in stricken sur-replies, that the striking orders were not identified in the notice of appeal or assignments of error, and that the Civil Rules do not provide for sur-replies.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio appellate authority on preservation of responsive arguments, the scope of a notice of appeal, and review of issues first developed in a stricken sur-reply is needed, along with the complete trial-court briefing.

judge_assessments.assessment: The general causation authority supports the proposition that a defendant's act need not be the sole or initial cause, and the summary-judgment standard requires an injury-specific evidentiary showing. The brief nevertheless does more than simply invoke chronology: it argues that the mortgage and release were part of an arrangement under which Lundberg expected the property not to remain security. The attack is effective to the extent Land Title never identifies Lundberg's precise damages or shows that none accrued between the February filing and March release. But the mere fact that the release came later does not itself establish an injury during that interval. The advocate risks remand if the claimed damages arose upon filing and were not eliminated by the later agreement.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief identifies the accommodation filing as the challenged act, says the mortgage is the sole basis of Lundberg's claims, cites authorities making proximate cause an element, and argues that Lundberg ultimately occupied the same unsecured position he chose when he signed and delivered the release.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The amended complaint, damages evidence, and chronology of any foreclosure, loss of priority, fees, or other injury are necessary to determine whether an injury accrued before or independently of the release.

judge_assessments.assessment: Reasonableness may be disputed, but this attack is secondary to the more fundamental absence of a manifestation by Equity Trust. If apparent authority fails for lack of principal conduct, the court need not decide whether Sheridan's reliance was reasonable. If a qualifying principal manifestation is found elsewhere in the record, the signed release, Lundberg's beneficial interest, delivery of the original, and the parties' ongoing business relationship could support reasonable reliance. The attack adds little independently on the present record.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on the release language, Lundberg's execution and delivery, Sheridan's testimony that he understood the release could be recorded, and the parties' alternative repayment arrangement.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The Equity Trust account documents and Sheridan's knowledge of the custodial arrangement would bear on reasonableness.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack correctly observes that the criminal forgery statute does not resolve whether a signature was unauthorized for civil purposes. But Land Title expressly assumes disputed wrongdoing for purposes of its independent causation argument. A court may affirm without deciding breach, falsity, or notarial misconduct if no cognizable injury was caused. These disputes become material only if the release-based no-injury theory fails; they do not independently defeat summary judgment. The advocate's use of the criminal definition is unnecessary and potentially distracting, but not outcome-determinative on the stated ground.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief acknowledges factual disputes over who signed and with what authority, then argues they are immaterial because causation fails even if Christine's version is assumed true. It relies on Gaudio for that assumed-wrongdoing causation analysis.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The elements and damages asserted under each tort count would show whether any claim makes unauthorized authentication independently actionable without consequential injury.

judge_assessments.assessment: The requested relief is imprecisely phrased, but this record does not support the attack's claim that the brief entirely ignores Christine's injuries. The brief repeatedly identifies her negligence and fraud claims, discusses her alleged unauthorized signature, invokes Gaudio, and argues that the release would remove the challenged lien from her property. It also references a separate contemporaneous answer brief addressing her cross-appeal. Whether those arguments are sufficient cannot be judged from the Lundberg-focused materials alone. A court would decide the assignments and parties actually before it rather than enlarge relief merely because of an overbroad concluding sentence.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief asks affirmance of the September 7 judgment as to both Lundberg and Christine, states that both parties' claims require proximate cause, discusses Christine's signature allegations, and incorporates or references a separate answer brief concerning her cross-appeal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Christine Sheridan's complaint, cross-appellate brief, Land Title's separate response, and the September 7 judgment are required to assess the permissible scope of disposition.

results.verdict: Partly persuasive on proximate cause, but vulnerable on auth
results.assessment: The brief has a workable no-injury theme because it can point to Lundberg’s signed, witnessed, notarized release, the later delivery of that document, and testimony that the parties had other repayment arrangements. But it is exposed in the places the challenges identify: apparent authority is not supported by any manifestation from Equity Trust, and the argument that release validity does not matter is too strained because validity and authority are predicates to the no-injury counterfactual. The standing fallback is also overbroad because it does not cleanly separate personal tort claims from injury to the mortgage interest. The preservation point is comparatively better, but not enough to cure the main doctrinal weakness.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief recites the Rule 56 standard but does not apply it claim by claim. Temple and the other authorities quoted require no genuine dispute, entitlement as a matter of law, and an adverse conclusion even after the evidence and inferences are viewed most strongly for the nonmovant. Yet the argument merely declares that the standard was met, without identifying the causes of action, their elements, the admissible Rule 56 materials negating those elements, or the substantive law governing ownership or entitlement to the urn and cremains. [u52-u55,u61,u72-u78]
challenges.why_it_matters: A correct abstract standard cannot substitute for demonstrating entitlement to judgment on each pleaded claim; the asserted legal conclusion remains unsupported.

target.excerpt: IV. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF DEFENDANT WHEN DEFENDANT MET ALL ELEMENTS IN THE STANDARD FOR REVIEW AND WAS ENTITLED TO SUMMARY JUDGMENT AS A MATTER OF LAW.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the central weakness in the defense of summary judgment. The cited cases accurately state the general Civ.R. 56 test, but the brief does not identify the pleaded claims and their elements, connect particular Civ.R. 56 materials to those elements, or explain why the substantive law makes the asserted facts dispositive. References elsewhere to exhibits and asserted undisputed facts provide some factual basis, but they do not supply the missing claim-by-claim legal analysis. Because review of summary judgment is de novo, the appellate court must independently determine entitlement to judgment; a conclusory assertion that the standard was met is not enough. The advocate risks losing affirmance if the record and appellant's briefing reveal a viable claim not negated by the cited evidence.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee satisfied Civ.R. 56 because Appellant's claims depended on an asserted legal interest in the urn and cremains, and the summary-judgment materials negated that premise. The brief shows that Appellant was never legally married to the decedent, did not pay the funeral expenses, and identified no admissible evidence establishing any title, contract, or other legally cognizable interest in the property. Viewing the evidence most strongly in Appellant's favor, reasonable minds could reach only one conclusion: Appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Replace the conclusory Civ.R. 56 paragraph with a claim-specific summary-judgment analysis tied to the record the brief actually describes. If the brief cannot identify the pleaded causes of action and the elements they require, it should narrow the argument to the property-interest theory shown in the brief rather than saying the standard was met in the abstract.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief assumes that lack of a legal marriage, nonpayment of funeral expenses, and payment by the decedent’s mother necessarily extinguished every legal or equitable claim to the urn or cremains. It cites no substantive authority establishing that marital status or payment alone controls ownership, possession, conversion, abandonment, or disposition rights. Its further assertion that six years of non-removal transferred ownership to Barney is likewise unsupported by any cited law. [u15,u20-u27]
challenges.why_it_matters: Without the governing substantive law, the asserted facts do not establish entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, even if undisputed.

target.excerpt: IV. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF DEFENDANT WHEN DEFENDANT MET ALL ELEMENTS IN THE STANDARD FOR REVIEW AND WAS ENTITLED TO SUMMARY JUDGMENT AS A MATTER OF LAW.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack lands squarely. The asserted facts may be relevant, but the brief does not establish the legal rules that make them dispositive. Lack of legal marriage may defeat a claim based specifically on surviving-spouse status, but it does not, without analysis, resolve every possible possessory, contractual, conversion, bailment, abandonment, or equitable theory. Likewise, payment of funeral expenses does not self-evidently establish ownership of the urn or exclusive control over remains, and the assertion that six years of non-removal transferred ownership to Barney is unsupported by cited law. The brief does not already answer this defect. The advocate risks losing the merits affirmance because undisputed facts alone do not support summary judgment unless substantive law makes them outcome-determinative.
challenges.suggested_response: On the claim actually pleaded and argued below, Appellant could not establish any cognizable right to the urn or cremains. The brief shows that he was never legally married to the decedent, that he paid none of the funeral bill, and that the funeral bill for the urn was paid in full by the decedent's mother. Appellant identified no admissible evidence of title, contract, or other legal entitlement superior to Appellee's. On this record, the trial court correctly entered judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that marital status, funeral-payment history, or six years of non-removal automatically extinguished every conceivable claim, and do not rely on the unsupported assertion that abandoned property transferred to Barney. The brief needs the governing substantive law for ownership or possession of the urn and cremains, or it must limit itself to the specific claim actually shown in the brief.

challenges.opponent_argument: The request to reverse the denial of vexatious-litigator relief principally lists proceedings and then labels them harassing. It does not set out and prove each requirement of R.C. 2323.52, explain how each listed matter qualifies under the statute, or show from admissible materials that the filings lacked legal or factual support or were brought merely to harass or maliciously injure. Several listed matters also involve different defendants, and one entry is a police-department matter rather than an identified civil action. [u81-u100]
challenges.why_it_matters: A count of filings, without a statutory element-by-element showing, does not establish entitlement to the extraordinary declaration or demonstrate that the trial court erred in denying it.

target.excerpt: V. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN FAILING TO GRANT DEFENDANT'S MOTION FOR SANCTIONS. WHICH INCLUDED DECLARING PLAINTIFF. WILFRED LOUIS ANDERSON. A VEXATIOUS LITIGATOR AS THAT TERM IS DEFINED IN OHIO REVISED CODE SECTION 2323.52.

challenges.judge_assessment: The statute supports focusing on whether the litigant habitually, persistently, and without reasonable grounds engaged in qualifying vexatious conduct, not merely on the number of proceedings. The brief uses some statutory language—harassment, malicious injury, lack of legal support—but mostly asserts conclusions and lists matters without demonstrating their dispositions, factual overlap, lack of reasonable grounds, or evidentiary basis. Different defendants do not necessarily prevent proceedings from showing a qualifying pattern, but the unexplained police-department matter and appellate proceeding cannot simply be counted as equivalent civil actions. The advocate risks affirmance of the denial because the record described does not compel a vexatious-litigator finding or establish reversible error under the applicable standard of review.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 2323.52 is designed to reach a party who, in multiple civil actions, habitually and persistently engages in conduct that lacks reasonable grounds and is intended to harass or maliciously injure an opponent. Appellant's filings, as recounted in this brief, all arise from the same cremains dispute and reflect repeated efforts to relitigate a claim for which he identified no legal entitlement. The trial court therefore erred in refusing to declare Appellant a vexatious litigator.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Add the statutory elements of R.C. 2323.52 and connect each listed filing to those elements, or narrow the request. A bare list of other cases and forums is not enough by itself to justify a vexatious-litigator declaration.

challenges.opponent_argument: Calling the motion “unopposed” does not itself satisfy Civ.R. 56. The brief’s own authorities state that judgment is proper only if the evidence leaves no genuine material dispute and, when viewed most strongly for the nonmovant, permits only an adverse conclusion. Thus the dispositive question remains whether the movant’s evidence carried that burden, not whether a response was filed. [u48-u55,u61,u76-u78]
challenges.why_it_matters: The trial court could not treat summary judgment as a default; absent a demonstrated evidentiary and legal basis, nonresponse does not cure the movant’s failure of proof.

target.excerpt: IV. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT IN FAVOR OF DEFENDANT WHEN DEFENDANT MET ALL ELEMENTS IN THE STANDARD FOR REVIEW AND WAS ENTITLED TO SUMMARY JUDGMENT AS A MATTER OF LAW.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a correct and consequential procedural point. The authorities quoted by the brief themselves require the movant to establish the Civ.R. 56 prerequisites; they do not authorize summary judgment merely because the opposing party filed no response. An unopposed motion permits the court to consider the movant's properly supported facts undisputed, but it does not convert summary judgment into default judgment or supply missing substantive entitlement. The brief partly answers the attack by saying the trial court reviewed the record, yet it never demonstrates what that review established. The advocate risks losing if the motion or affidavits did not carry the initial Rule 56 burden.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant's failure to file a timely response did not relieve the trial court of its Civ.R. 56 duty, but Appellee carried that burden. The motion was supported by sworn affidavits and documentary exhibits showing the absence of any legally cognizable claim to the urn and cremains, while Appellant filed no timely Civ.R. 56 evidence creating a genuine issue of material fact. Under Temple, Mers, and Williams, reasonable minds could reach but one conclusion adverse to Appellant.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Acknowledge that an unopposed motion is not a default, then show the sworn materials and undisputed facts that satisfied the movant's Rule 56 burden. The brief should make clear that the ruling rested on the evidentiary record, not on Appellant's failure to respond.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief seeks both a vexatious-litigator declaration under R.C. 2323.52 and unspecified monetary sanctions, but supplies no separate rule, statute, standard of review, calculation, or evidentiary basis for a monetary award. Its conclusion that two years of litigation warrants money sanctions does not identify recoverable fees or losses or establish the prerequisites for that distinct remedy. [u100,u102]
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if some conduct could support prospective vexatious-litigator restrictions, the requested monetary reversal is independently unsupported and cannot be awarded merely by invoking R.C. 2323.52.

target.excerpt: V. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN FAILING TO GRANT DEFENDANT'S MOTION FOR SANCTIONS. WHICH INCLUDED DECLARING PLAINTIFF. WILFRED LOUIS ANDERSON. A VEXATIOUS LITIGATOR AS THAT TERM IS DEFINED IN OHIO REVISED CODE SECTION 2323.52.

challenges.judge_assessment: The request for monetary sanctions is independently underdeveloped. The brief invokes R.C. 2323.52 for the vexatious-litigator declaration but identifies no distinct statutory or rule-based basis for money sanctions, no governing standard, no recoverable categories, and no evidence or calculation of loss or fees. Even if the conduct justified prospective filing restrictions, that would not automatically establish an appellate entitlement to an unspecified monetary award. The advocate risks complete denial of the monetary component and, because the requested amount and findings are absent, has not shown what judgment the appellate court could properly direct.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee respectfully requests the declaration authorized by R.C. 2323.52 and such other relief as the statute specifically permits. Appellee does not separately press an unspecified monetary award on the present record, because no independent legal basis or evidentiary calculation for that award has been developed here.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Drop the unsupported request for unspecified monetary sanctions unless the brief can cite a distinct rule or statute and support a specific amount with evidence. On the present record, the safe course is to seek only the relief actually authorized by the authority cited.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief answers only whether the affiant signed before a commissioned notary, not whether fraud was practiced on the court. Notary licensure and certification may bear on execution or signature authenticity, but they do not establish that the affidavit’s factual contents were true, that it was genuinely executed by the identified notary, or that no intentional deception occurred. The brief supplies no authority defining fraud upon the court or connecting R.C. Chapter 147 compliance to defeat that theory. [u31-u34]
challenges.why_it_matters: If notarization is not dispositive of fraud, the brief has not supplied the governing test or shown that the trial court correctly rejected the fraud theory.

target.excerpt: I. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN FAILING TO FIND DEFENDANT COMMITTED FRAUD UPON THE COURT WHEN DEFENDANT SUBMITTED AN AFFIDAVIT SIGNED BY A LICENSED NOTARY IN THE STATE OF OHIO.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack correctly identifies a gap in the brief's reasoning: compliance with notarial formalities does not, by itself, resolve whether an affidavit contained intentional falsehoods or was used to corrupt the judicial process. R.C. Chapter 147 addresses notarial authority and acts; the brief cites no fraud-upon-the-court standard and does not apply one. But the attack overreaches insofar as it assumes the appellant challenged the affidavit's factual truth rather than only the seal or signature. On this record, the brief may prevail if the alleged fraud was limited to facial notarial defects and the appellant supplied no evidence of deception. The advocate nevertheless risks having the fraud discussion treated as legally incomplete rather than as an adequate independent basis for affirmance.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant's first assignment attacks only the form of the notarization. But a licensed Ohio notary's certificate and seal satisfy Chapter 147, and Appellant cites no authority or admissible evidence showing that any alleged irregularity in the notarial act amounted to fraud upon the court. The trial court therefore did not err in declining to disregard the affidavit on that ground.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Separate the notarization issue from the fraud-upon-the-court theory. If the brief keeps the fraud label, it needs a fraud-upon-the-court standard; if it does not have one, it should confine itself to the facial notarization point shown in the record.

challenges.opponent_argument: The contention that the notary’s signature was not forged rests on the notary’s commission status and the document’s notarized appearance. But a valid commission through December 9, 2013 does not prove that the commissioned person actually placed the challenged signature on these January 9 affidavits. The brief identifies no testimony, affidavit from the notary, signature comparison, or other evidence establishing genuineness. [u37]

target.excerpt: II. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN FAILING TO FIND DEFENDANT COMMITED FRAUD UPON THE COURT WHEN THE NOTARY SIGNATURE APPEARING IN DEFENDANT'S PLEADING WAS NOT FORGED.

challenges.judge_assessment: A valid commission does not logically prove that the commissioned notary personally signed a particular document, so the brief's affirmative assertion that the signature was not forged is not established merely by licensure and facial notarization. That is a real evidentiary gap. It may not be outcome-determinative, however, because the record described identifies no evidence supporting forgery, the affidavits were facially notarized, and the appellant did not timely oppose summary judgment. The party alleging forgery cannot create a genuine issue through accusation alone. The advocate risks losing the categorical no-forgery rationale, but not necessarily affirmance if the challenger failed to produce or preserve any evidence of forgery.
challenges.suggested_response: The record identified in this brief shows that the affidavits were notarized by a licensed Ohio notary, and Appellant points to no affidavit from the notary, no handwriting evidence, and no other admissible proof that the signature was forged. A valid commission and facial notarization are not the sole basis of Appellee's position, but Appellant's bare accusation is not enough to defeat summary judgment. The trial court correctly declined to find forgery or fraud on that basis.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not say the notary's commission alone proves the signature was not forged. Instead, argue that Appellant identified no admissible evidence of forgery and therefore failed to create a genuine issue of material fact.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief answers only whether the affiant signed before a commissioned notary, not whether fraud was practiced on the court. Notary licensure and certification may bear on execution or signature authenticity, but they do not establish that the affidavit’s factual contents were true, that it was genuinely executed by the identified notary, or that no intentional deception occurred. The brief supplies no authority defining fraud upon the court or connecting R.C. Chapter 147 compliance to defeat that theory. [u31-u34]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If notarization is not dispositive of fraud, the brief has not supplied the governing test or shown that the trial court correctly rejected the fraud theory.

attacks_proposed.argument: The contention that the notary’s signature was not forged rests on the notary’s commission status and the document’s notarized appearance. But a valid commission through December 9, 2013 does not prove that the commissioned person actually placed the challenged signature on these January 9 affidavits. The brief identifies no testimony, affidavit from the notary, signature comparison, or other evidence establishing genuineness. [u37]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without evidence linking the signature to the commissioned notary, the premise that there was no forgery—and therefore no fraud—is unsupported.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief conflates three distinct questions: whether the notary held a commission, whether the signature was authentic, and whether the affidavits were admissible Rule 56 evidence. Licensure resolves only authority to perform a notarization; it does not logically resolve authorship of the signature or the evidentiary sufficiency of the affidavits. [u37]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The court cannot affirm the handling of a forgery allegation merely by accepting proof of the notary’s licensure.

attacks_proposed.argument: The claimed failure to file a timely summary-judgment response does not itself prove that the notary signature was genuine. The docket language quoted by the brief establishes a response deadline, but the brief cites no authority making nonresponse an admission of signature authenticity or a waiver of a fraud/forgery challenge on appeal. [u41-u43]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If nonresponse does not establish genuineness, the brief must prevail on competent evidence rather than procedural default, and it identifies none directed to authorship of the signature.

attacks_proposed.argument: The no-pretrial argument depends entirely on the premise that summary judgment disposed of the case, yet the brief itself says summary judgment was granted only “in part.” It does not identify which claims or issues remained after that partial ruling, provide the pretrial order or governing local rule, or show that no unresolved matter required further proceedings. [u46-u49,u68-u69]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without showing that the partial judgment eliminated every issue otherwise set for pretrial, courtroom efficiency alone does not answer the asserted procedural error.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief recites the Rule 56 standard but does not apply it claim by claim. Temple and the other authorities quoted require no genuine dispute, entitlement as a matter of law, and an adverse conclusion even after the evidence and inferences are viewed most strongly for the nonmovant. Yet the argument merely declares that the standard was met, without identifying the causes of action, their elements, the admissible Rule 56 materials negating those elements, or the substantive law governing ownership or entitlement to the urn and cremains. [u52-u55,u61,u72-u78]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A correct abstract standard cannot substitute for demonstrating entitlement to judgment on each pleaded claim; the asserted legal conclusion remains unsupported.

attacks_proposed.argument: Calling the motion “unopposed” does not itself satisfy Civ.R. 56. The brief’s own authorities state that judgment is proper only if the evidence leaves no genuine material dispute and, when viewed most strongly for the nonmovant, permits only an adverse conclusion. Thus the dispositive question remains whether the movant’s evidence carried that burden, not whether a response was filed. [u48-u55,u61,u76-u78]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The trial court could not treat summary judgment as a default; absent a demonstrated evidentiary and legal basis, nonresponse does not cure the movant’s failure of proof.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief assumes that lack of a legal marriage, nonpayment of funeral expenses, and payment by the decedent’s mother necessarily extinguished every legal or equitable claim to the urn or cremains. It cites no substantive authority establishing that marital status or payment alone controls ownership, possession, conversion, abandonment, or disposition rights. Its further assertion that six years of non-removal transferred ownership to Barney is likewise unsupported by any cited law. [u15,u20-u27]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without the governing substantive law, the asserted facts do not establish entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, even if undisputed.

attacks_proposed.argument: The request to reverse the denial of vexatious-litigator relief principally lists proceedings and then labels them harassing. It does not set out and prove each requirement of R.C. 2323.52, explain how each listed matter qualifies under the statute, or show from admissible materials that the filings lacked legal or factual support or were brought merely to harass or maliciously injure. Several listed matters also involve different defendants, and one entry is a police-department matter rather than an identified civil action. [u81-u100]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: A count of filings, without a statutory element-by-element showing, does not establish entitlement to the extraordinary declaration or demonstrate that the trial court erred in denying it.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief seeks both a vexatious-litigator declaration under R.C. 2323.52 and unspecified monetary sanctions, but supplies no separate rule, statute, standard of review, calculation, or evidentiary basis for a monetary award. Its conclusion that two years of litigation warrants money sanctions does not identify recoverable fees or losses or establish the prerequisites for that distinct remedy. [u100,u102]
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even if some conduct could support prospective vexatious-litigator restrictions, the requested monetary reversal is independently unsupported and cannot be awarded merely by invoking R.C. 2323.52.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the central weakness in the defense of summary judgment. The cited cases accurately state the general Civ.R. 56 test, but the brief does not identify the pleaded claims and their elements, connect particular Civ.R. 56 materials to those elements, or explain why the substantive law makes the asserted facts dispositive. References elsewhere to exhibits and asserted undisputed facts provide some factual basis, but they do not supply the missing claim-by-claim legal analysis. Because review of summary judgment is de novo, the appellate court must independently determine entitlement to judgment; a conclusory assertion that the standard was met is not enough. The advocate risks losing affirmance if the record and appellant's briefing reveal a viable claim not negated by the cited evidence.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief recites the three-part Civ.R. 56 standard from Temple and Delker, adds the favorable-inference rule from Mers and Williams, references facts concerning marriage, payment, abandonment, and burial, and then states that Appellee met the standard and that the unopposed motion was properly granted.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complaint, summary-judgment motion and exhibits, trial court's complete judgment entry, and substantive Ohio law governing each pleaded claim would determine whether the judgment can nevertheless be affirmed from the record.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack lands squarely. The asserted facts may be relevant, but the brief does not establish the legal rules that make them dispositive. Lack of legal marriage may defeat a claim based specifically on surviving-spouse status, but it does not, without analysis, resolve every possible possessory, contractual, conversion, bailment, abandonment, or equitable theory. Likewise, payment of funeral expenses does not self-evidently establish ownership of the urn or exclusive control over remains, and the assertion that six years of non-removal transferred ownership to Barney is unsupported by cited law. The brief does not already answer this defect. The advocate risks losing the merits affirmance because undisputed facts alone do not support summary judgment unless substantive law makes them outcome-determinative.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief asserts that Appellant was never legally married to the decedent, defaulted on the funeral-home contract, paid none of the funeral expenses, and left property at Barney's residence for more than six years. It concludes that Appellant had no legal or equitable entitlement and that Barney acquired anything abandoned.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research should identify the causes of action actually pleaded and the Ohio law in effect at the relevant time governing disposition of cremated remains, ownership or possession of an urn, conversion, contractual rights, and abandonment of personal property.

judge_assessments.assessment: The statute supports focusing on whether the litigant habitually, persistently, and without reasonable grounds engaged in qualifying vexatious conduct, not merely on the number of proceedings. The brief uses some statutory language—harassment, malicious injury, lack of legal support—but mostly asserts conclusions and lists matters without demonstrating their dispositions, factual overlap, lack of reasonable grounds, or evidentiary basis. Different defendants do not necessarily prevent proceedings from showing a qualifying pattern, but the unexplained police-department matter and appellate proceeding cannot simply be counted as equivalent civil actions. The advocate risks affirmance of the denial because the record described does not compel a vexatious-litigator finding or establish reversible error under the applicable standard of review.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief alleges at least eight forums, lists several cases involving Mitchell, the funeral home, and Cleveland Heights, recounts a prosecutor's warning concerning alleged harassment, and asserts that the filings were unsupported and intended to harass or maliciously injure Mitchell.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The precise 2013 version of R.C. 2323.52, the sanctions motion and supporting evidence, records and dispositions of the listed proceedings, the trial court's reasons, and appellate decisions addressing the standard of review would settle the issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a correct and consequential procedural point. The authorities quoted by the brief themselves require the movant to establish the Civ.R. 56 prerequisites; they do not authorize summary judgment merely because the opposing party filed no response. An unopposed motion permits the court to consider the movant's properly supported facts undisputed, but it does not convert summary judgment into default judgment or supply missing substantive entitlement. The brief partly answers the attack by saying the trial court reviewed the record, yet it never demonstrates what that review established. The advocate risks losing if the motion or affidavits did not carry the initial Rule 56 burden.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief repeatedly calls the motion unopposed, recites the Civ.R. 56 standard, says the trial court reviewed all facts presented, and concludes that the motion was well taken.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete summary-judgment motion, supporting materials, and judgment entry are necessary to determine whether the movant independently satisfied Civ.R. 56 despite the absence of a timely opposition.

judge_assessments.assessment: The request for monetary sanctions is independently underdeveloped. The brief invokes R.C. 2323.52 for the vexatious-litigator declaration but identifies no distinct statutory or rule-based basis for money sanctions, no governing standard, no recoverable categories, and no evidence or calculation of loss or fees. Even if the conduct justified prospective filing restrictions, that would not automatically establish an appellate entitlement to an unspecified monetary award. The advocate risks complete denial of the monetary component and, because the requested amount and findings are absent, has not shown what judgment the appellate court could properly direct.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief asserts that two years of unwarranted and harmful litigation justified sanctions, including monetary sanctions, and asks for reversal of the denial. It supplies no separate monetary-sanctions analysis or calculation.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The sanctions motion, the authority invoked below, evidence of fees or losses, the trial court's ruling, and the sanctions provisions in effect in 2013 would determine whether any monetary relief was preserved and legally available.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack correctly identifies a gap in the brief's reasoning: compliance with notarial formalities does not, by itself, resolve whether an affidavit contained intentional falsehoods or was used to corrupt the judicial process. R.C. Chapter 147 addresses notarial authority and acts; the brief cites no fraud-upon-the-court standard and does not apply one. But the attack overreaches insofar as it assumes the appellant challenged the affidavit's factual truth rather than only the seal or signature. On this record, the brief may prevail if the alleged fraud was limited to facial notarial defects and the appellant supplied no evidence of deception. The advocate nevertheless risks having the fraud discussion treated as legally incomplete rather than as an adequate independent basis for affirmance.

Chapter 147, states that the notary's certification authenticates the signature, notes that the notary was commissioned and a seal was present, and concludes that any seal issue did not affect the affidavit's legality or the summary-judgment ruling.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The appellant's exact fraud allegation, the challenged affidavits, the trial court's ruling, and Ohio authority defining fraud upon the court would determine whether the brief's narrow notarization response fully addresses the preserved issue.

That is a real evidentiary gap. It may not be outcome-determinative, however, because the record described identifies no evidence supporting forgery, the affidavits were facially notarized, and the appellant did not timely oppose summary judgment. The party alleging forgery cannot create a genuine issue through accusation alone. The advocate risks losing the categorical no-forgery rationale, but not necessarily affirmance if the challenger failed to produce or preserve any evidence of forgery.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the affidavits contained Ohio's legal requirements, the notary's commission remained valid through December 9, 2013, the trial court accepted their format, and Appellant failed to file a timely response after receiving an extension.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The affidavits, any signature exemplars or notary testimony, the appellant's trial-court filings, and the precise basis of the forgery allegation would determine whether a genuine authenticity dispute existed.

judge_assessments.assessment: The conceptual distinction is sound, but as an attack it substantially duplicates a2 and a6. The brief does conflate commission status with authenticity, yet it does not rely solely on commission status to establish Rule 56 admissibility; it also invokes the certifications, facial format, trial court review, and absence of a timely response. The court would address the concrete evidentiary and summary-judgment questions rather than treat this framing criticism as a separate ground.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on the notary's valid commission, the affidavits' facial compliance, the trial court's acceptance of their format, and Appellant's failure to respond.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The same record materials identified for a2 and a6 would resolve the underlying issues.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack correctly observes that nonresponse does not affirmatively prove that a signature is genuine, but it misreads the brief's procedural point. The brief says Appellant waived the opportunity to file a timely opposition and that the court could rule on the existing record; it does not clearly claim that silence constituted a factual admission of genuineness. Failure to oppose may leave a facially regular affidavit unrebutted even though it does not independently authenticate a disputed signature. The court would likely resolve this through preservation and the sufficiency of the existing evidence, making this attack largely duplicative of a2 and a7.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes the response deadline, says Appellant failed to file an appropriate response after obtaining an extension, and concludes that he waived the opportunity to respond and that the court properly ruled on the pending motions.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The docket and the contents of all filings made by the response deadline would show whether the authenticity issue was actually raised and preserved.

judge_assessments.assessment: The phrase granting summary judgment 'in part' creates some ambiguity, but the attack assumes without record support that merits claims remained pending. In context, the brief immediately contrasts the summary-judgment disposition with the same entry's denial of the separate sanctions motion, and the case proceeded as a final appeal. A court generally would not infer unresolved claims merely from this wording. The absence of a cited pretrial authority is a briefing weakness, but if summary judgment entered final judgment on the merits, no pretrial remained necessary. The attack would become material only if the judgment entry actually left claims unresolved or a governing order required a pretrial notwithstanding final disposition.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that summary judgment was granted 'in part,' that sanctions were denied in the same ruling, that the summary-judgment motion was unopposed and appropriate, and that no pretrial was necessary after summary judgment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The complete April 11, 2013 judgment entry, docket, case-management order, and applicable Cuyahoga County local rules would eliminate the ambiguity.

results.verdict: partly persuasive on the procedural points but weak on the m
results.assessment: The brief is strongest where it reminds the court that an unopposed motion still had to satisfy Civ.R. 56 and where it points to facial notarial compliance as a rebuttal to a narrow fraud attack. But it is not yet persuasive on the issues that matter most: it does not analyze the pleaded claims element by element, it does not supply the substantive law showing why the marriage and funeral-payment facts are dispositive, and it does not support the vexatious-litigator or monetary-sanctions requests with the required separate showings. The fraud-upon-the-court and forgery arguments also remain evidentiary thin. The research does not cure those gaps.

On this record, Appellant failed to meet his reciprocal burden under Civ.R. 56 to point to evidence supporting entitlement to the property.

challenges.judge_assessment: The governing point is sound: an unopposed motion is not automatically granted, and the movant retains the initial Civ.R. 56 burden. The attack overstates the brief's deficiency somewhat because the statement of facts identifies particular exhibits, including affidavits, a death certificate, a funeral bill, a check, and a clergy statement. Still, the argument section largely recites the standard and announces that it was met without analyzing the claims or the admissibility and effect of those materials. Under Civ.R. 56, once Appellee supported the motion with evidentiary materials showing the absence of a genuine issue of material fact, Appellant was required to respond with specific facts demonstrating a triable issue. He did not do so, and the trial court properly granted summary judgment on the record before it.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that the motion was granted merely because it was unopposed. Recast this point to say Appellee satisfied the initial Civ.R. 56 burden with the evidentiary materials attached to the motion, and Appellant then failed to come forward with specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial.

target.excerpt: I. THE TRIAL COURT DID NOT ERR IN FAILING TO FIND DEFENDANT COMMITTED FRAUD UPON THE COURT WHEN DEFENDANT SUBMITTED AN AFFIDAVIT SIGNED BY A LICENSED NOTARY IN THE STATE OF OHIO.

legal_sources.title: CMHA v. Barry Gauntt et al.
legal_sources.citation: 2014 CVG 001938 (Cleveland Mun. Ct., Housing Div. Nov. 24-25, 2014)

challenges.judge_assessment: The logical criticism is valid: proper notarization authenticates the notarial act or signature; it does not by itself establish the truth of every factual statement or categorically defeat fraud upon the court. The brief does not state the elements of fraud upon the court or apply them. Source 73 supports only the separate summary-judgment burden and does not establish the scope of Ohio's fraud-upon-the-court doctrine. The force of the attack depends on Appellant's actual theory. If the alleged fraud rested only on a supposedly invalid seal, expired commission, or forged notary signature, the brief's response may be adequate. If the allegation concerned false affidavit contents or a fabricated oath, the brief leaves a material gap.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s fraud argument rests on a challenge to the affidavit’s authenticity, not on any record evidence that the affidavit was improperly executed. The affidavit was notarized by a licensed Ohio notary, and Appellant identified no admissible evidence that the notarization was forged or that the affidavit was not sworn in accordance with Ohio law. On that record, the trial court had no basis to disregard the affidavit in ruling on summary judgment.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the answer focused on authentication, not on proving the truth of the affidavit’s contents. The brief should say the alleged fraud theory failed because the affidavit was executed before a licensed Ohio notary and Appellant identified no admissible evidence that the notarization was forged or that the affidavit was not sworn as represented.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief asserts that the notary’s signature was not forged, but identifies no evidence affirmatively establishing that proposition. The notary’s license expiration date would show only that the commission allegedly remained active on the stated date; it does not itself prove who signed the certification or that the oath was administered as represented. A Rule 56 movant must point to evidence affirmatively demonstrating the absence of the asserted factual issue. [73]
challenges.why_it_matters: The Court cannot convert an unsupported assertion of nonforgery into an undisputed fact merely because Appellant did not file the response Appellee expected.

They concern eviction appeals, voluntary relinquishment of possession, and recognized mootness exceptions. They neither establish that a recorded quiet-title judgment remains reversible nor refute Ohio doctrine concerning satisfaction or execution of judgments. No record-based exception to mootness is identified. The brief's categorical phrasing is broader than its supporting analysis, but these authorities do not supply a basis for rejecting the result in this case.

They also treat appeal, stay, and mootness as separate questions. Nothing cited by the brief shows that the recorder’s ministerial acceptance of a judgment eliminates the appellate court’s ability to reverse that judgment and restore the prior title status.
